The Big Flaw in Big Law
Major law firms in the United States seem to be enjoying a golden age. Partners’ individual compensation is well into the millions — star partners may make $20 to $30 million annually — and even first-year lawyers earn $250,000 at top New York City firms.
Then, in October, the well-known firm of Weil, Gotshal & Manges announced that it would dissolve, an implosion that shocked the bar. Unlike other firms that have collapsed, Weil was large (about 1,200 lawyers), highly respected and scandal free. Yet its own leadership surrendered, and stopped trying to save this 95-year old firm.
Why? Let’s begin with the fact that law firms are composed of often contentious persons (called lawyers) who are inclined to argue their positions aggressively. These disputes — typically about compensation or control issues — can produce rivalries and bitterness, but they have virtually never been the primary reason a major firm voluntarily dissolved itself.
The Weil implosion highlights the new internal stresses destabilizing large law firms today, making them look more like collections of free agents — many of whom are waiting for a better offer to lure them away. Firms not only have to compete zealously at practicing law, but also at holding a highly mobile team together — much as if every player on the Dodgers or Yankees were a free agent who could leave tomorrow.
Increasingly, compensation packages for partners reflect the principle of eat what you kill, and the once-respected ideals such as firm culture, the community of the partnership and a commitment to pro bono work and public service are recognized more in rhetoric than in practice. Particularly for young lawyers, the future looks foreboding as artificial intelligence reduces the need for humans in the handling of routine legal work.
In the past, big law firms maintained stability by offering all partners with the same seniority equal compensation. It was inefficient but broadcast the message that the partnership was a band of equals, each committed to the firm’s advancement.
